newsitem.title: USA: El Paso CSD No. 11, Colo., TANs SP-1-plus - S&P.
newsitem.headline: El Paso CSD No. 11, Colo., TANs SP-1-plus - S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, Sept 10 - Standard & Poor's Corp Tuesday said it has assigned its SP-1'-plus rating to El Paso County School District No. 11 (Colorado Springs), Colo.'s TANs series 1996 due June 30, 1997, which will sell Sept. 11, 1996.
-- The pledge of fiscal 1997 general fund ad valorem tax revenues securing the notes;
-- Segregation of funds to repay the notes, with good projected cash coverage of debt service at the set-aside dates; and

The TANs are payable from ad valorem taxes to be received for district general fund operations during fiscal 1997. The district will establish a separate repayment account within the general fund, into which it will set aside net tax revenue for the payment of principal and interest on the notes. The district expects to receive 35% of its projected $53.6 million fiscal 1997 property tax revenue in March 1997 and 30% in May 1997. In each of those months, the district intends to deposit property tax collections sufficient to pay 50% of the TAN principal and interest into the repayment account. Coverage of the applicable note debt service amounts by net general fund cash balances at the end of each of the two segregation months is projected to be 1.33 times (x) and 1.15x, with overall coverage at maturity projected at 1.51x. Coverage levels based solely on property tax revenues received in each of the set-aside months are comparable at 1.37x and 1.62x, with overall coverage at maturity projected at 2.29x.

The district has a history of conservative cash flow projections, enabling it to set aside 100% of debt service on its series 1995 TRANs in March, ahead of the projected 50%-50% March and May set-aside schedule. The current $22.7 million series 1996 TRAN borrowing is a significant increase from the prior year's $14.5 million borrowing. The increase can be attributed primarily to a one-time payroll cycle change and increased charter school expenditures.

The district's finances are sound. State aid, allocated based on enrollment, provides slightly over half of the district's operating revenue. The district's fiscal 1995 ending general fund balance totaled $11.2 million, or 8.3% of expenditures, including a state-mandated emergency reserve equal to 3% of annual general fund spending. Unaudited 1996 results indicate a $572,000 reduction in the general fund balance, following three consecutive years of operating surpluses. The drawdown, the result of increased spending on capital projects and repairs associated with rapid enrollment growth, was necessitated by the district's failure to pass a bond issue for capital needs in November, 1995. The district plans to put the $99.8 million bond issue to the voters again in November, 1996.

Note proceeds and the note repayment fund shall be deposited in a restricted account within the district's general fund. Standard & Poor's has reviewed the district's investment portfolio and has determined that as of Aug. 31, 1996 it meets Standard & Poor's guidelines for investment of municipal issuers' operating funds. As of Aug. 31, 1996, the market value of the portfolio was $26.4 million as compared to the book value of $26.4 million. The weighted average maturity is 112 days, well under the recommended maximum of one year. Approximately 85% of the portfolio is invested in U.S. treasuries or U.S. agencies, Standard & Poor's said.
